engine_name: RunPod driver upgrade (Infrastructure Option, not an inference engine). Strategy: move off the current pod (driver 570.195, CUDA 12.8 ceiling) onto a RunPod machine whose HOST driver is >=575.51 (for CUDA 12.9) or >=580 (for CUDA 13.0), so that stock pre-built CUDA 12.9/13.0 wheels of vLLM/PyTorch run without a source build. Mechanism is RunPod's 'Allowed CUDA Versions' filter at deploy time, NOT a special template name. Researched as of 2026-06-17.
cuda_128_compatible: N/A for the option itself (this IS about escaping the 12.8 ceiling). Clarification of the premise: the limiting factor is the HOST NVIDIA driver, which lives on the physical machine and CANNOT be changed from inside a RunPod pod (the driver is injected by nvidia-container-toolkit from the host). Driver->CUDA runtime ceilings: 570.x -> CUDA 12.8; >=575.51 -> CUDA 12.9; >=580 -> CUDA 13.0. NVIDIA datacenter driver 575.57.08 shipped Jun 2025; 580.65.06 (Aug 2025) through 580.126.x (Jan-Feb 2026) are current. So the only way to raise the CUDA ceiling on RunPod is to land on a machine that already has a newer host driver; you select that with the deploy-time CUDA filter. Note: CUDA minor-version compat means a 12.8-host can still RUN many cu12.x runtimes via forward-compat libs, but to use cu129/cu130 wheels cleanly you want the matching host driver. [uncertain] exact lowest driver RunPod guarantees per GPU/datacenter at any given moment (it varies by machine and is not published).
gemma4_support: N/A (engine-agnostic infrastructure). This option does not itself add or remove Gemma 4 support; it provides the CUDA 12.9/13.0 host driver so that whichever engine you run (stock vLLM cu129/cu130 wheel, etc.) gets Gemma 4 support from that engine. The A6000 (sm_86, Ampere) remains the GPU; google/gemma-4-31B-it at 4-bit (W4A16 / NVFP4 / bitsandbytes) fits the 48GB card the same as before. A newer driver does NOT change model format requirements (safetensors for vLLM).
per_request_reasoning_toggle: N/A (engine-agnostic). Per-request reasoning toggling is a property of the serving engine (e.g. vLLM gemma4 reasoning parser with enable_thinking / reasoning_effort), not of the RunPod driver. Upgrading the driver does not by itself enable this; it enables running the stock vLLM wheel that DOES provide it, instead of being stuck on a 12.8-only build.
per_request_reasoning_budget: N/A (engine-agnostic). reasoning_budget / thinking_token_budget capping is a vLLM feature (PR #37112). The driver upgrade's relevance is indirect: it lets you install the stock cu129/cu130 vLLM wheel that ships this feature, rather than building vLLM from source on the 12.8 host. The capability comes from vLLM, not from the driver.
tool_calling_support: N/A (engine-agnostic). Gemma 4 tool calling is handled by the engine (vLLM --tool-call-parser gemma4). The driver upgrade does not affect tool-call parsing; it only removes the CUDA-ceiling reason for building vLLM from source. Whichever vLLM build you end up running provides (or fails to provide) tool calling identically on driver 570 vs 580.
openai_api_compatible: N/A (engine-agnostic). The OpenAI /v1/chat/completions endpoint is provided by the engine (vLLM/llama.cpp), unaffected by the host driver. RunPod exposes the pod via its HTTP proxy or a TCP port mapping regardless of driver version.
continuous_batching: N/A (engine-agnostic). Continuous batching is a vLLM/engine capability, independent of the RunPod host driver.
installation_steps:
How to actually GET a newer-driver pod on RunPod (this is the operative procedure for this option):

1) Web console -> Deploy -> select RTX A6000 -> click 'Filters' (a.k.a. Advanced Filters) -> set 'Allowed CUDA Versions' to 12.9 and/or 13.0. This restricts the machine pool to hosts whose driver supports that CUDA runtime (>=575.51 for 12.9, >=580 for 13.0). There is NO dedicated 'A6000 driver-580 template' name; you constrain the HOST via this filter and then pick any container image (e.g. runpod/pytorch:...-cu1300-... or your own).

2) Pick an image that matches: RunPod publishes runpod/pytorch with cu1300 tags (e.g. 1.0.3-cu1300-torch291-ubuntu2404) and a runpod/comfyui:cuda13.0 template; or bring a custom image. The host driver (from the filter) must be >= the image's CUDA requirement.

3) CLI caveat: `runpodctl pod create` has NO CUDA/driver filter yet (open feature request runpodctl#253 '--min-cuda-version'). Use the web UI or the GraphQL/REST API GPU-availability filtering to constrain driver/CUDA. Deploying blind via CLI can land you on a 570 host again.

4) Verify after boot: `nvidia-smi` (top-right shows Driver Version and 'CUDA Version' = max supported) should read >=580 / 13.0. If it shows 570/12.8, terminate and redeploy with the filter applied.

There is no in-pod way to upgrade the driver; you must redeploy onto a different host.
serve_command:
N/A as a serve command (infrastructure option). Once on a >=580 / CUDA-13.0 host you would serve with the STOCK vLLM wheel, e.g.:

UV_TORCH_BACKEND=cu130 uv pip install 'vllm>=0.20.0'   # default PyPI wheel is cu130 in v0.20.0+
vllm serve google/gemma-4-31B-it-qat-w4a16-ct --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --max-model-len 16384 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser gemma4 --reasoning-parser gemma4 --chat-template examples/tool_chat_template_gemma4.jinja

The point of the driver upgrade is that this stock cu130 (or cu129) install just works, removing the need to compile vLLM against cu128. NOTE: even on cu128 today, vLLM publishes cu128 wheels (see vLLM_from_source result), so the driver upgrade is NOT strictly required to run stock vLLM; it is required only if you specifically want the cu129/cu130 default wheels or CUDA-13-only features.
speculative_decoding: N/A (engine-agnostic). Speculative decoding (vLLM MTP, llama.cpp draft) is unaffected by the host driver. No change from the upgrade.
known_issues_gemma4:
Gotchas specific to the RunPod driver-upgrade path (the real findings):

(A) CONTAINER LIMITATION IS ARCHITECTURAL, NOT TEMPLATE/DRIVER-SPECIFIC. Standard RunPod Pods (Secure Cloud and Community Cloud) are themselves CONTAINERS, not VMs/hosts. NET_ADMIN, custom seccomp profiles, --privileged, and Docker-in-Docker / nested containers are blocked by RunPod's pod runtime, not by the pod template or the driver. A newer-driver pod is STILL a container and will have the SAME restrictions. Therefore a driver upgrade WILL NOT fix the no-container / NET_ADMIN / seccomp problem. To get those you need a fundamentally different product: RunPod BARE METAL (full physical server, no hypervisor, no container layer, kernel/driver control, root) -- or a community provider that explicitly offers 'privileged' GPU pods (e.g. QuickPod flags privileged offers; some RunPod community hosts may expose privileged mode, but it is per-offer and not guaranteed). Instant Clusters are containerized too and do NOT give system-level customization. So: driver upgrade unlocks newer CUDA; it does NOT unlock containers/NET_ADMIN/seccomp.

(B) NETWORK VOLUME LOCKS YOU TO A DATACENTER. A network volume (the way to persist /workspace across pod swaps) is bound to one dataCenterId. You can freely re-attach it to a DIFFERENT GPU type / pod / template WITHIN THE SAME DATACENTER -- so switching from your current A6000 pod to a newer-driver A6000 pod preserves /workspace IF both are in the same DC and the volume is attached at deploy time (it replaces the default /workspace, mounted at /workspace, Secure Cloud only). It CANNOT be attached/detached after deploy. If the only newer-driver A6000 machines are in a different datacenter than your existing volume, data does NOT auto-sync; you must rsync / use the S3 API / runpodctl between two bridge pods to migrate. So data preservation is conditional on datacenter co-location.

(C) runpodctl has no CUDA/driver filter (issue #253) -> CLI deploys can silently land on a 570 host.

(D) Driver availability per GPU type is not published and fluctuates; newer drivers cluster on newer GPUs (5090/H100/H200/B200). A6000 is older Ampere, so >=580 hosts for A6000 specifically may be scarcer -- verify availability with the CUDA filter before relying on it.
vram_usage: N/A (unchanged by driver). A6000 is still 48GB; google/gemma-4-31B-it at W4A16/NVFP4 ~18-20GB weights + KV cache at 16k, with room for bge embedder (~0.13GB) + bge-reranker-v2-m3 (~2.3GB). The driver upgrade does not change VRAM math.
small_scale_fit: Reasonable IF the goal is purely 'run stock cu129/cu130 wheels without compiling'. For a 1-dev + <=10 concurrent-user setup, redeploying an A6000 pod with the CUDA filter set to 12.9/13.0 is low-effort (web UI checkbox), and pricing is the same A6000 rate. BUT note: stock vLLM already ships cu128 wheels, so for vLLM specifically the driver upgrade may be UNNECESSARY -- the cheaper win is just `uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=cu128` on the current pod. The driver upgrade is the easiest path ONLY for engines/wheels that have NO cu128 build, or if you hit a genuine CUDA-13-only requirement. The operational risks (datacenter relock of the network volume, A6000 newer-driver scarcity, CLI cannot filter) are mild but real for a small team.
overall_recommendation: VIABLE (situational) -- and it does NOT solve the container problem. Answers to the 5 questions: (1) No special A6000 'driver-580 template' exists; you request a newer driver by setting 'Allowed CUDA Versions' = 12.9/13.0 in Deploy -> Filters on the web UI (GraphQL/REST can also filter; runpodctl cannot yet, issue #253). Pair with any image (e.g. runpod/pytorch cu1300 tag or custom). (2) COST: essentially the SAME -- A6000 is billed by GPU type, not driver; ~$0.33-0.49/hr Community, +~$0.10-0.40/hr Secure Cloud. No driver premium. (3) The no-container / NET_ADMIN / seccomp limitation is a RunPod-WIDE property of the containerized Pod runtime, NOT this pod template and NOT the driver -- a newer-driver pod is still a container with the SAME restrictions, so it will NOT fix containers. To get NET_ADMIN/seccomp/nested containers you must move to RunPod BARE METAL (root, kernel control) or a community provider's explicitly 'privileged' offer. (4) /workspace CAN be preserved via a network volume, but the volume is locked to one datacenter; you can move it to a new A6000 pod/template only within the same DC (attach at deploy, replaces /workspace). Cross-DC requires manual rsync/S3/runpodctl migration. (5) Is it the easiest path to unlock STOCK vLLM vs building from source? Usually NO -- stock vLLM already publishes cu128 wheels that run on driver 570.195, so the simplest unlock is `uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=cu128` on the CURRENT pod (no redeploy, no driver change). The driver upgrade is only the easiest path if your target wheel/engine lacks a cu128 build or needs CUDA 13 specifically. PROS: trivial to request (UI filter), zero cost delta, removes any cu129/cu130 wheel friction. CONS: does not fix containers (the user's apparent root pain), can relock the network volume to a datacenter, newer-driver A6000 hosts may be scarce, CLI can't filter so easy to mis-deploy, and it's likely unnecessary for stock vLLM which has cu128 wheels. RECOMMENDATION: if the real blocker is engine wheels, first try cu128 stock vLLM on the existing pod; only upgrade the driver if a cu129/cu130-only requirement appears. If the real blocker is containers/NET_ADMIN/seccomp, the driver upgrade is the WRONG tool -- go Bare Metal.
